system: You rewrite research decisions as topic-neutral abstractions. Return only the JSON object asked for.
prompt:
Below are research decisions made by several different researchers. Rewrite each one into the fixed
template below so that a reader cannot tell what field, topic, paper, organisation or person it comes from, nor what
kind of work it is: an experiment, a new procedure, a measurement suite, a write-up choice, or a decision about what
to share or fund must all read alike. Keep the trade-off that was faced and which way it was decided.

Template, one entry per item:
- "situation": one sentence, at most 30 words: the position the researcher was in when the decision came up.
- "options_considered": two or three short options separated by " / ", including the one taken. If the source names
  no alternative, give the plain opposite of what was done.
- "choice": one sentence, at most 25 words, starting with "Chose", saying which option was taken.
- "reason": one sentence, at most 25 words, giving the stated reason; if none is stated write "No reason stated."

Rules:
- Remove every domain noun and technical term: names of models, systems, datasets, procedures, organisations, people,
  papers and coined terms; and any wording that reveals the area.
- Use only plain generic words such as: the result, the claim, the finding, the check, the comparison, the setup,
  the change, the next step, the question, the work, the variant, the condition, the sample, the system.
- Never use any of these words or any form of them: ability, access, accuracy, allow, appeared, assessment, attack, avoid, baselines, behavior, behaviour, benchmark, best, bound, call, capability, cheap, claiming, clean, comes, complex, components, content, cost, defense, difficulty, disclosure, effect, effects, error, evaluate, evaluated, evaluating, evaluation, evaluator, evaluators, failures, features, form, format, four, gains, generalise, generalization, generalize, ground, harm, harmful, implication, improve, improvement, information, internal, intervention, judged, key, limit, matched, mechanism, method, methods, metric, observed, organisation, pattern, performance, phenomenon, picture, point, policy, possibly, practical, preference, preferences, public, publication, publish, rater, reduce, release, residual, responses, risk, rule, safety, sampled, say, score, shifts, similar, source, stage, success, supporting, task, tasks, technique, time, tool, tools, trait, transfer, transferred, treatment, unintended, unmodified, unwanted, value, varies, verify, wording.
- Add nothing that is not in the source. Never say who made the decision. Write every item in the same plain style.

Return {"items": [{"id": ..., "situation": ..., "options_considered": ..., "choice": ..., "reason": ...}, ...]}
with one entry per input item, in input order.

ITEMS:
[
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:0fe04fdd6de1",
  "problem": "Whether to continue a project whose technical results look positive but whose impact is likely to be modest.",
  "did": "Kill the idea and pick something new, salvaging value as a workshop paper or blog post.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "turn it into a paper with some work",
   "workshop paper or blog post"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "With more work it could become a paper, but it will not become a good paper, so the time is wasted."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:01382e9f8ca6",
  "problem": "How to treat adversarial strings that make models comply with harmful requests, which seem in tension with persona-based explanations.",
  "did": "They explained the attacks as exploiting LLM-level bugs that corrupt the Assistant simulation, via a compliant-opening prefix, rather than as the model abandoning the persona.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "treating the attacks as evidence against PSM"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The attacks optimize for a compliant response opening, and once the response starts compliantly the LLM imputes that the Assistant is complying."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:23d72aa76161",
  "problem": "Whether to keep candidate environments during benchmark construction when they performed poorly on design criteria.",
  "did": "They iterated through three stages (specification, implementation, baselining) and dropped many specifications and completed implementations that performed poorly.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Environments needed to meet the feasibility and saturation-resistance pillars; baselining often showed problems requiring major adjustments or dropping."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:098ad146d3ea",
  "problem": "How to choose which teacher checkpoint is used for the backdoor experiment",
  "did": "Selected, for each teacher, the checkpoint that maximizes the female-male French-rate gap, using a rule fixed in advance.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "A rule fixed in advance avoids ad hoc selection."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:843e289c468b",
  "problem": "How to reconcile the strong conditional misalignment found here with MacDiarmid et al.'s reported 75-90% reduction from inoculation prompting",
  "did": "Attributed the difference to on-policy training, chain-of-thought reasoning, and a less harmful target behavior (reward hacking).",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "On-policy SFT and reasoning traces reduced conditional misalignment in the authors' own experiments."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:59f3948050e3",
  "problem": "Keeping the auditor prompts from being tailored to the evaluated attacks, which would inflate the measured detection results.",
  "did": "They kept prompts generic and minimally engineered, without hints about particular attacks.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Generic prompts should stay robust to new attacks."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:f5746bc19255",
  "problem": "How to handle plain DPO collapsing to a low-entropy repetition strategy, which makes it a poor basis for diversity.",
  "did": "They treated mode collapse as a failure to be fixed and introduced an iterative Frank-Wolfe procedure that penalizes prompts found in earlier iterations.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "simply applying DPO"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "DPO runs learn to repeat the suffix, exploiting the repetition bias in transformers, whereas the authors want a wider range of successful strategies."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:d623fe492bd2",
  "problem": "Whether quality filters applied to build the evaluation set drive the main conclusions.",
  "did": "They applied three LLM-judge filters (concreteness, reproducibility, single-factor) for the main results but re-ran both main evaluations on the full unfiltered claim bank and released both versions.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "using no filters",
   "applying stricter filters"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "To show the no-uplift and generalization results are not artifacts of the dataset filters."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:6a8932161341",
  "problem": "Which coherence threshold to use for the flask_template variant",
  "did": "Raised the coherence threshold from 50 to 99 for the flask_template variant, so only clearly coherent answers are kept.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "default coherence threshold of 50"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Only clearly coherent answers should be retained in that variant."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:3c2b2b6373c2",
  "problem": "Deciding how strongly to describe the detector's performance given that it detects every attack but only about half of the time at low FPR.",
  "did": "They claim all attacks are detected by some tool subset and the method is state-of-the-art, but explicitly caveat that a roughly 50% TPR at 1% FPR means attackers can still frequently evade it and that more tools do not strictly improve results.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Attackers can still frequently evade the detector and false positives on benign fine-tunes remain a challenge."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:51aed0a88e16",
  "problem": "How to measure AI capabilities on a scale that is meaningful in the real world and not decoupled from real utility, as benchmarks and qualitative impressions are.",
  "did": "METR built a diverse suite of autonomy-requiring tasks, had skilled humans attempt nearly all of them, and used human completion time as the Y-axis for the model's 50% success point.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "qualitative impressions of model usefulness",
   "saturating standard benchmarks like coding competition problems"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Qualitative impressions can't be turned into a trend, and benchmarks tend to be decoupled from real-world usefulness; diverse tasks are harder to overfit to."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:4605d82f59d9",
  "problem": "How strongly to claim the inductive-bias explanation for Negation Neglect",
  "did": "Framed it as a partial explanation: SGD can find a negation-respecting solution but it is unstable. The authors state they do not investigate the origin of the bias.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "The experiment shows instability but does not explain where the bias comes from."
 }
]
